text: Welcome to the Beginner Capstone. Over these ten lessons you're going to take one real stakeholder request, all the way from a vague hallway ask to a published Power BI report. Lesson one starts where every real project actually starts: before any SQL, before any Power BI, with a conversation.

Here's the ask. The Southeast regional sales manager at Carraway Supply Company stops by your desk and says, can you put together something simple showing how sales are doing by region and product line this quarter? I just need to glance at it before our Monday call. Sounds easy. It isn't, yet — because four phrases in that sentence are each hiding a real question. This quarter — calendar or fiscal, to date or the whole thing? By region — every territory, or just this manager's? How sales are doing — revenue, order count, or both? Product line — category, subcategory, or something broader?

The fix isn't guessing. It's a short follow-up conversation that nails down four things: the time window, the scope, the metric, and the grouping. Five minutes spent here saves you from building the wrong thing and finding out on Monday morning, in front of the stakeholder.

Once you ask, the vague request turns into something specific — a report showing total sales amount and order count for the current quarter, broken out by sales territory and product line, for the Southeast manager, ready before Monday's call. That sentence is the real spec for this entire project. Notice it's specific enough that a teammate could read it and build the same thing you would.

Just as important as what's in scope is what's deliberately left out. In scope: one quarter, one T-SQL query, one Power BI report with a couple of visuals. Out of scope: a multi-year trend, a data warehouse, any kind of ETL pipeline. Matching your effort to the actual ask is part of doing this well.

That's the business ask, turned into a real requirement. Next lesson, we start translating that requirement into a plan for the T-SQL query itself — which tables you'll need, and how they join together, sketched out before a single line of real SQL gets written.
